recordings.text: A fork works because one move can only answer so much. Here a single piece attacks several targets together, so one reply may not be enough to cover them all.

Before each move, it helps to ask which squares the opponent's pieces can reach next. This move gives them a fork: a single piece of theirs can then reach several targets together. Spotting that piece first is the habit to build.

A different move had a fork in it, one piece attacking several targets together. That idea goes unused in the game. When comparing candidates, a forcing move that hits two things deserves to be checked first.
A pinned piece is tied to whatever stands behind it. This move pins a piece to its king, so it can't step off that line without exposing the king. That restriction is what the move is built on.

Pieces lined up with their own king are always worth a second glance. This move lets the other side pin one of them, and a piece pinned to its king can't leave that line without exposing the king. It pays to check those lines before moving, not after.

A piece could have been pinned to its king by a different move. Pinned that way, it couldn't have left its line without exposing the king, and that restriction would have been the point. Instead, no pin happens in the game.

Think of a skewer as a line attack read from front to back. The front piece is attacked first, and if it steps aside, the piece behind it is exposed on the same line. Notice how the order of the pieces on that line does the work.

When two pieces share a line, an attack on the first can reach the second. The other side now has a skewer: if the front piece gives way, the piece behind it could come under attack. Shared lines like that are worth checking before each move.

A different move offered a skewer, attacking a front piece with another standing behind it on the same line. If the front piece had moved off that line, the piece standing behind it would have been exposed to the attack. In the game, that line is never used.
A defender only protects something while it stays on the board. This move captures one, and whatever it was guarding may lose its protection. So the real target is what stood behind the defender.

Every defender is also a target. This move lets the other side capture one, and whatever it protects could then be left uncovered. Before moving, it's worth knowing which piece is holding things together.

Another move could have captured a defender, and what it was guarding would have lost its protection. Instead, that defender stays on the board. A defender is often the right target, because taking it weakens something else.

A king behind its own pieces can find every escape square blocked by its own side. That's the back-rank mate idea in this move: the king is boxed in with no room to step out. Its own cover is what limits it.

A king needs at least one free square off its back rank. This move lets the other side aim for a back-rank mate, because the king is hemmed in by its own pieces. The king's escape squares are the first thing to check here.

The enemy king had no square off its back rank, which made a back-rank mate idea possible here. In the game, the idea goes by. When a king has no escape square, checks along its back rank deserve a careful look.

A pawn that reaches the last rank becomes a new piece, which is why every step toward it matters. This move is about that route to promotion. Count the squares the pawn still needs, and what could stop it.

An advanced pawn changes what every other piece has to do. After this move, the other side has a chance to promote, so one of their pawns may get through to the last rank. Count its steps first, then look for what could block it.
A stronger move offered a route to promotion, a pawn heading for the last rank. Instead, the pawn stays where it stands. When a pawn is close, counting its steps should come before quieter plans.

Sometimes the most important piece in a move is the one that doesn't move. Here one piece steps out of the way and uncovers an attack from the piece behind it. So read the line it opens, not just the square it lands on.

A piece that blocks another's line can uncover an attack just by moving. This move lets the other side do exactly that, a discovered attack from the piece behind. Check which lines their next move could open.

One of the other candidates was a discovered attack: one piece moving aside so the piece behind it could attack. Here that line never opens. When two pieces of one side share a line, moving the front one is worth considering.
One move can make two threats, and a single reply often can't meet both. This move is built around exactly that kind of double attack. Name each threat in turn, then see why they work together.

When the opponent can make two threats at once, one answer may not cover both. This move gives them that double attack. So the useful check, before moving, is what their most forcing reply would attack.
A stronger move made two threats at once, and this move doesn't. Double attacks are worth looking for early, because one reply may not be able to handle both.

A defender can only be in one place. This move pulls a defender away from its job, a deflection, and what it was guarding is left open. Look first at what the defender was covering, then at what drew it away.
A defender with an important job can be lured away from it. That's exactly the deflection this move allows the other side. Ask what that defender is covering now, and what could pull it off.
Another move could have drawn a defender away from what it was guarding, a deflection. This move doesn't. The idea to keep: a defender that's drawn away leaves its job undone.
The simplest gains come from pieces nobody is guarding. A piece with no defender at all is captured here. Checking for loose pieces first saves a lot of calculation later.
Another move could have taken an undefended piece, and this move leaves it there. A quick scan for unguarded pieces is a sensible first step before anything more ambitious.

A piece without a defender can be taken for nothing. This move leaves a piece in that state, and the other side can capture it. The habit that prevents this is simple: before each move, check what's unguarded.

When a defender leaves its post, its protection leaves with it. This move takes away a piece's only real defender, so the other side can now capture what it was guarding. So before a defender moves, it's worth knowing what depends on it.

Each opponent move can create a new threat, so it's worth asking what it changed. The opponent's previous move attacked a piece, and this move doesn't respond to that, so the piece can now be captured. Asking it after every opponent move is the habit to build.

Every exchange comes in two halves: what is taken and what comes back. Here the capture is answered by a recapture that takes a more valuable piece. So count the whole exchange, recapture included, before judging the first capture.
A piece on its starting square has few squares to work with. This move brings a minor piece off its original square and into play. Notice where it stands now and what it can reach.
A minor piece could have been developed with a different move, coming off its starting square for the first time. That's worth comparing with the move played, especially in the early part of a game.
A rook works best along a file that nothing blocks. This move leaves a rook on an open file, with no pawns of either color on it, so the whole file is available to it.
A rook could have reached an open file, where neither side has a pawn, if a different move had been played. Rooks tend to be most useful on files like that, which is why the comparison matters.
A semi-open file has none of a side's own pawns, but at least one enemy pawn. This move leaves a rook on a file like that, so it faces an enemy pawn rather than one of its own.
A different move would have given a rook a semi-open file, clear of its own pawns yet still holding at least one enemy pawn. The difference lies in whose pawns stand on the file.
A pawn is passed when no enemy pawn stands ahead of it on its own file or either neighboring file. This move leaves a pawn like that. No enemy pawn can stop it on the way forward, so only pieces can.
Another move would have created a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or the files beside it. A pawn like that can only be stopped by pieces, which is why it's worth noticing.
A passed pawn matters more with every step it takes. This move brings an already passed pawn nearer the last rank. Count how many squares remain before it promotes.
The passed pawn could have stepped forward with a different move. Comparing the two, notice how much closer to promotion it could have come.
An isolated pawn has no friendly pawn on either neighboring file, so no pawn is able to defend it. This move leaves one. Any protection for it would have to come from the pieces.
A different choice would have isolated a pawn, leaving it with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file. Without pawn neighbors, defending it would fall to the pieces.
A piece with a defender can't simply be taken for free. This move gives a piece support it didn't have, so a capture on that square could now be answered with a recapture.
Another move would have given a piece a defender, so it wouldn't have been standing unprotected. Support like that is worth comparing with what the played move did instead.

Having no defender describes a piece's situation; it doesn't mean the piece is lost. Once this move is made, one piece stands with no defender. Whether it can actually be won depends on what can reach it.
Had a different move been played, one piece would have had no defender at all. That alone wouldn't mean the piece could be won, but it's a detail worth tracking.
A king is safer with a square to step to. This move opens a legal flight square it didn't have before. Notice which piece moved out of its path.
A different move would have opened a new legal square for the king. Check which piece would have had to move to make that room.
Castling is the one move that relocates two pieces at once. Here the king castles and the rook moves next to it. Check both new squares when you compare positions.
Castling was available instead, and it would have moved king and rook together in one turn. Comparing it with the move played shows what each choice did for the king.
Two bishops together cover both square colors. This capture breaks up a bishop pair, so one square color is now left without a bishop on that side.
A different move would have taken a bishop, and with it the opposing bishop pair. That would have left the other side with bishops on only one square color.
Pawns on the same file can't protect each other. This move leaves doubled pawns, two of one color on a single file. Notice that the front pawn also blocks the one behind it.
A different move would have doubled a side's pawns, putting two of one color on a single file. Pawns stacked like that can't defend each other, which is the detail to weigh.
This move opens the way to a forced checkmate. The way to understand it is to take the attack one forcing move at a time. Start with the first check or capture, and find where the defense runs out.
When a forced checkmate exists, it outweighs every other idea on the board. There was one here, and this move lets it go. Look at the checks first; that's usually where a finish begins.
A sacrifice is only sound if it holds up after the material is taken. This one does, in the line we checked. So the reason for it lies in what happens after the capture, not in the material count.
Sometimes a position allows exactly one answer. This move alone held the position among those we checked, and each of the others was losing. It's worth keeping as a defensive example.
An advantage can slip away with a single imprecise move. Here, every alternative we checked was losing, and this move alone kept the advantage. Precision mattered here more than usual.
The first question after any move is what the reply can take. In this position, the other side has a capture at once. Start with that capture before looking at anything quieter.
A check must be answered before any other plan. The strongest reply here gives check, so that's where the analysis has to begin.
Comparing two moves on the board teaches more than looking at either one alone. Here the engine would choose another move. Play both, and notice how the replies differ.
A move's cost is measured against what was available. The engine rates this one below its best option. To see why, compare the replies to each; the gap shows up there.
This is a strong choice, judged against everything the engine examined. What makes it worth keeping is the reason behind it.
This is sound, though the engine would choose differently. It keeps much of what the position offered, and comparing the two moves shows where the difference lies.
Opening theory recognizes the line this move belongs to. Recognition tells us which line this is; it doesn't grade the move.
Here the game leaves the line our opening book recognizes. From this point on, the decisions rest on the position itself, so the reasons behind each move matter more.

A setback isn't final while the position can still be held. The earlier setback no longer decides things, because this move makes the position playable. Connecting those two moments is the useful part of the lesson.
Despite the earlier setback, there's a playable position again after this move. Errors by the other side helped make that possible, so the recovery belongs to both players' choices.
An opponent's error only helps if the reply makes use of it. This move puts to use the opportunity the opponent's last move offered. Keeping those two moves together is what makes the lesson stick.
There was an opportunity in the opponent's last move, and this move doesn't take it. Returning to the position before it, and asking what that move changed, is the way to find it.
We've seen this problem before in this game. When the same issue repeats, there's usually one habit underneath it, and comparing the moments helps find it.
The unguarded piece from earlier has a defender now. Comparing the two positions shows exactly where its protection came back from.
Positions often slip through several small concessions rather than one big error. This is one of a series that has worsened the position together, so the sequence matters as much as this move.
Keeping an advantage takes as much care as winning one. The reviewed moves held it all the way to the recorded win, and following that stretch shows how it was kept.
The same issue turns up in other saved games as well. A pattern across several games points to a habit, and a habit is something practice can change.
Checkmate: the king is attacked and has no legal escape. Reviewing the last few moves is a good way to keep the pattern.
The king is checkmated, with no legal square left to escape to. The useful lesson lies earlier, at the point where the defense could still have changed course.
This game finishes as a draw. A result can be settled while the decisions inside the game still have something to teach.
Look the position over carefully, piece by piece, and choose your move when it's clear to you.
As it stands, that try doesn't solve the position. Try to see why first, then pick a different move.
The attempt produced no result this time. It's fine to play the move again.
According to the saved engine analysis, this move leads to a forced checkmate for the side that played it. That's the main point to understand.
The saved engine analysis shows a forced checkmate for the other side after this move. Everything else in the line matters less than that.

At the finish of the saved line, the side that made this move is down material compared with where it started.

The pawn is promoted, and the new piece delivers checkmate, leaving the king nowhere legal to go.
Promoting on the last rank also gets the pawn's own king out of check.
This move removes a piece by capturing it.
A piece is captured, and the same move gives check.
A piece is captured, and the move is checkmate, leaving the king with no legal escape.
A piece is captured, and that capture also takes the king out of check.
When the pawn captures on the last rank, it also promotes.
Capturing on the last rank, the pawn is promoted, and the new piece gives check.
Capturing on the last rank, the pawn is promoted, and the result is checkmate, with no legal escape for the king.
Capturing on the last rank, the pawn is promoted, and in doing so it gets its king out of check.
The king castles, and the rook, on its new square, gives check.
The king castles, and the rook on its new square delivers checkmate, with no legal escape for the opposing king.
One piece attacks several targets, and in this example it goes on to take one of them. The line also ends with a net gain in material for that side.
The marked capture isn't available: the piece is pinned to its king, and moving off the line would leave its own king in check.
Because the attacked piece is pinned to its king, it can only move along the pin line, if it can move at all.
Here the capture succeeds because its defenders are pinned to their king and can't take back. By the time the line shown is over, that side is ahead in material.
The pinned piece can't step off its line without exposing the king, so it stays where it is. As the moves play out, it's captured there.
When the front piece moves off the line, the piece behind it is exposed, and it's captured along that same line.
The king is in check and has to step off the line. The piece behind it is then exposed, and the same attacker takes it.
The capture sequence starts with the lone defender. With it gone, the piece it was guarding is taken next in these moves.
Drawn away from what it was guarding, the defender leaves a piece unprotected, and that piece is then captured.
Moving the blocking piece opens a line for the piece behind it, which then makes the capture.
One piece moves out of the way, and the piece behind it now gives check.
This is double check: two pieces check the king at once, so only a king move can answer it.
The moving piece makes one attack and uncovers a second from the piece behind it. In this example, the second attacker is the one that captures.
Here promotion goes together with a net material gain for that side, as the example finishes.
Nothing defends that piece, so it can be taken without a recapture, and this example ends with that side ahead in material.
The key change came from the opponent's previous move, which freed the attacking piece from a relative pin. The target was then left in place, and in the line shown it's captured.
The other side is entitled to play the reply marked on the board. Playing it out yourself is the clearest way to see what it does.
A useful habit: before moving, find every piece of yours that could be captured with no good recapture.
Before settling on a quiet move, scan for enemy pieces that nothing is guarding.
Among the forcing moves, look for one piece that can attack two valuable targets together.
A pinned piece is shielding something. Before moving it, check whether that's your king or a more valuable piece.
When an attack lands on one piece, look along the same line for a valuable piece standing behind it.
A defender may be guarding more than it seems, so before exchanging it, list what it protects.
When a piece blocks a line, ask what would be uncovered if it moved.
Look for a single move that makes two threats, remembering that checks and newly opened lines count as threats too.
Before a back-rank defender leaves, make sure your king still has a square to escape to.
Count the squares each advanced pawn needs to promote, and consider the pawn moves that force a reply.
Every defender has a list of duties. Before moving one, check which pieces would lose its protection.
Weigh the first capture against the recapture that follows, since both belong to the same exchange.
A forcing exchange can lure a defender off its other duties, so look for that before anything quieter.

These moves show how play could go if the replies are strong. That's an illustration, not a claim that each reply is forced.

Let's begin at the start and work through the game step by step. There's no hurry; we'll give each idea the time it deserves.
Hello, I'm Alfie. We'll take things one step at a time, and I'll explain the reason behind each idea, not just the move.
Something worth knowing about this position: apart from the pawns, only the knights can move yet, and every pawn move opens a path for another piece.
Material is a resource, and here a piece is invested soundly. That's what makes this move brilliant.
A brilliant move. Notice the order: the cost is paid at once, and the checked line shows it was affordable.
Counting material is usually the first step. This move is a reminder that it isn't the last one.
Brilliant. The checked line has an answer to the capture, and replaying it shows how the idea works.
Strength at the right moment is worth more than strength at any other. This move shows it.
On an ordinary turn, this would simply be a strong move. On a turn this important, it's a great one.
Great. This is a move to keep: a strong choice, at one of the game's important moments.
Great. Look first at how much depended on the choice here, then at the move itself: a strong one.
This is the engine's top choice, which makes it the measure for every other move here.
Best. Nothing here improves on it, which a few alternatives on the board will confirm.
Best. Accurate moves teach as much as errors do, so this one is worth a slow replay.
The best move here. Best doesn't have to mean dramatic, only the most accurate available.
A good move. Sound moves are the foundation; the sharpest ones are a refinement on top.
A good move. The top choice is a little stronger, and working out why makes a useful small exercise.
Good. Sound, and close to the top choice, which went a little further.
Good. Being sound and being the top choice are two different things, and this move is the first.
A small inaccuracy. The best move kept a little more, and the difference repays one careful look.
This is the smallest kind of error, an inaccuracy. A little value is given up, nothing more.
An inaccuracy. Small differences like this are easiest to see with both moves side by side.
Here the position slips a little. It helps to ask what the move gives up, even when it's small.
A mistake. The useful question is what this move gives up that the engine's choice keeps.
A mistake. It's larger than a slip, so the mechanism behind it deserves some care.
Mistakes are judged by what changes, not by how a move looks. After this one, the position is clearly worse.
A real error. The engine's choice and this one lead to quite different positions.
Chances deserve the same study as errors. One was here, and this move doesn't use it.
The position just before this move is worth setting up again. A better opportunity was waiting there.
A missed chance. A mistake is about what a move gives up; a miss is about what it doesn't take.
A chance goes unused here. The move itself is less important than the one that wasn't played.
A blunder: the most serious grade there is, and so the most important kind to study.
This changes the position a great deal. Big swings like this are worth taking apart step by step.
A severe error. With the engine's choice set beside it, the full size of the damage comes into view.
Here the balance swings sharply. Studying a blunder starts with the reply that follows it.
Legal, yes, though the lesson has another move in mind. Try a different one.
